tips.title: Merger is agreed, takeover is bought
tips.body: A **merger** is two businesses **agreeing** to join. A **takeover** is one buying a **controlling interest** in another, which may be hostile. Use Edexcel's pairs: internal (organic) and external (inorganic).

tips.title: Internal finance is retained profit and selling assets
tips.body: Only those two are **internal**. Loans and shares, including a stock market flotation, are **external**. Retained profit is what is left after tax **and** after dividends, not just profit.

tips.title: A tariff is a tax on imports
tips.body: Charged by the country the goods **arrive** in, which makes the imported product dearer than a local one. Not a tax on exporting.

steps.title: Why a business grows, and the two routes
steps.body:
A business grows to win a bigger **share of the market**, to spread its fixed costs over more output, and to make itself harder to compete with. Growth is not automatically good, and that is the judgement the long questions want.

Edexcel splits growth into two routes, and expects both names:

- **Internal growth**, also called **organic growth**. The business grows **itself**, by selling more of what it makes or by making something new.
- **External growth**, also called **inorganic growth**. The business grows by **joining with another business**, through a **merger** or a **takeover**.

The difference matters because the two routes carry completely different risks. Organic growth is slow and cheap and stays under control. External growth is fast and expensive and brings someone else's problems with it.

check.prompt: A bakery opens three more shops of its own. What kind of growth is this?

steps.title: Internal growth: the business grows itself
steps.body:
Edexcel names two ways a business grows organically, and each has sub-routes worth learning by name.

**New products.** The business sells something it did not sell before, through **innovation** and **research and development**. This is slow and costly, and most new products fail, but what succeeds belongs entirely to the business.

**New markets.** The business sells its existing product to people who do not currently buy it, by:

- **changing the marketing mix**, for instance a lower price or a different promotion aimed at a new group of customers
- **taking advantage of technology**, above all selling online to people it could never reach from a shop
- **expanding overseas**, selling the same product in another country

The attraction of organic growth is **control**. The business keeps its own culture, its own way of working and all of the profit. The drawback is that it is **slow**, and a competitor growing by takeover can overtake it.

steps.title: External growth: merger, takeover, and becoming a plc
steps.body:
External growth means growing by **joining with another business**. Edexcel names two forms, and the difference between them is a common one-mark question.

- A **merger** is an **agreement** between two businesses to join together and become one new business. Both sides want it.
- A **takeover** is one business **buying a controlling interest** in another, which means more than half of its shares. The business being bought may not want it, in which case the takeover is hostile.

External growth is **fast**: a business buys market share, customers, staff and premises in one move rather than building them over years. It is also **expensive**, and it often disappoints, because two workforces used to different ways of working do not always fit together.

**Becoming a plc.** A growing business may become a **public limited company**, whose shares can be bought by anyone on the stock market. Edexcel names this as the ownership type for growing businesses. Going public raises large amounts of money, but the original owners **lose control**, since anyone can buy the shares, and the accounts become public for competitors to read.

steps.title: Paying for growth: where the money comes from
steps.body:
Growth has to be financed, and Edexcel splits the sources into **internal** and **external**.

**Internal sources** come from inside the business:

- **retained profit**: profit kept back after tax and after paying dividends to the owners
- **selling assets**: turning something the business owns but no longer needs, such as an old building or machinery, into cash

**External sources** come from outside:

- **loan capital**: borrowing, repaid with interest
- **share capital**: selling shares in the business, including **stock market flotation** for a public limited company

Internal sources cost no interest and give nothing away, but there is only so much of them. External sources can raise far more, at the cost of interest or of ownership.

steps.title: Why aims and objectives change
steps.body:
A business does not keep the same aims for ever. Edexcel names **five** reasons they change as a business evolves, and a question naming one expects you to explain the chain that follows from it.

- **Market conditions.** Demand falls in a recession, or a new competitor arrives, so an aim of growth may become an aim of survival.
- **Technology.** Customers move online, so an aim of opening more shops becomes an aim of building an e-commerce site.
- **Performance.** A business doing better than expected raises its sights; one doing worse cuts back.
- **Legislation.** A new law, for instance on packaging or emissions, forces a change in what the business aims to do.
- **Internal reasons.** The owner's own plans change: a founder wanting to retire, or to sell, or simply to work fewer hours.

Notice where each comes from: **market conditions**, **technology** and **legislation** come from outside the business, while **performance** and **internal reasons** come from inside it.

steps.title: How aims and objectives change
steps.body:
Edexcel also names **how** the aims change, and these are the four the mark scheme looks for:

- a **focus on survival or growth**, swapping one for the other
- **entering or exiting markets**, starting to sell somewhere new or pulling out
- **growing or reducing the workforce**
- **increasing or decreasing the product range**

Each of these cuts both ways, and the direction depends on what caused the change. A business doing well **enters** a market, hires and widens its range. One in trouble **exits**, cuts staff and narrows down to what sells.

When Rivelin Cycles decided to grow, its workforce went from **42** to **58**, a rise of **16** people, and it entered the German market. Had the recession hit instead, the same four headings would have moved the other way.

steps.title: Globalisation: what it does to a business
steps.body:
**Globalisation** is the way national economies have become linked into one world market, so a business in Sheffield competes with one in Shenzhen. Edexcel names four effects.

- **Imports.** Two things at once: **competition from overseas** selling into the home market, and the chance to **buy from overseas** more cheaply.
- **Exports.** **Selling to overseas markets**, which multiplies the customers available but brings new costs and rules.
- **Changing business locations.** Production moves to where costs are lower, or nearer to the customers who buy it.
- **Multinationals.** Businesses with operations in more than one country, which can move production, and profit, to wherever suits them.

Businesses **compete internationally** in two ways Edexcel names: through the **internet and e-commerce**, which lets a small business sell abroad without any premises there, and by **changing the marketing mix** for each country, such as a different price, a translated name or a different promotion.

steps.title: Barriers to trade: tariffs and trade blocs
steps.body:
Selling abroad is not free. Edexcel names two barriers.

A **tariff** is a **tax on imports**, charged by the country the goods arrive in. It makes the imported product dearer, so home-produced goods look cheaper by comparison. That is the point of it.

A **trade bloc** is a group of countries that have agreed to trade freely **with each other**, usually with no tariffs inside the bloc and a common tariff on goods coming in from outside. A business inside the bloc trades freely; one outside pays to get in.

steps.title: Ethics, the environment and pressure groups
steps.body:
The last part of 2.1 is the one students answer most loosely, and it is all about **trade-offs**.

**Ethical considerations** are about doing what is right: paying suppliers fairly, not using child labour, being honest in advertising. The trade-off Edexcel names is **between ethics and profit**. Paying a fair price for coffee beans costs more than paying the lowest price available. A business does it anyway because customers value it, and because the damage from being caught behaving badly can be far larger than the saving.

**Environmental considerations** are about the damage the business does: emissions, packaging, waste, the distance goods travel. The trade-off here is **between the environment, sustainability and profit**. Recyclable packaging costs more per unit. **Sustainability** means meeting today's needs without stopping future generations meeting theirs, so it is a long-term view set against a short-term cost.

**Pressure groups** are organisations that campaign to change what businesses do, and Edexcel asks specifically about their **impact on the marketing mix**. A campaign can force a business to change its **product**, for instance reformulating to cut sugar, its **promotion**, if an advert is judged irresponsible, its **price**, and its **place**, if a retailer drops it.

steps.title: Going deeper: building a 12-mark 'evaluate' answer
steps.body:
The 12 marker is where Business grades are decided, and it has a shape the mark scheme rewards.

**Two developed chains, one each way.** A chain is a *because … which means … so …* sentence that ends at the business. "A flotation raises a large sum **because** shares are sold to the public, **which means** the factory can be built without borrowing, **so** no interest is payable if sales are slow."

**Applied throughout.** Not "businesses" but *this* business, using the numbers and details given. Quote them.

**A judgement that depends on something.** The top level wants a conclusion that is **valid and well reasoned**, which in practice means saying **what it depends on** and **how the answer would change**. "Floating is the better choice **if** the owners are willing to give up control; **if** keeping control matters more to them than the interest, the loan is better despite the cost."

Balance is not the same as sitting on the fence. Give both sides, then come down on one.

visuals.problem: *A manufacturer can fund £830,000 of a £2,000,000 factory internally. Evaluate whether it should raise the £1,170,000 shortfall by flotation or by a loan.* (12 marks)

steps.text: *A flotation raises the whole shortfall in one go and no interest is payable, so if the new factory is slow to fill, the business is not forced into repayments it cannot meet.* — level 2
steps.note: a chain, ending at the business

steps.text: *It also raises more than the £830,000 the business could find internally, so the factory can go ahead this year rather than in three years' time.* — level 3
steps.note: applied to the figures in the case

steps.text: *Against that, floating means anyone can buy the shares, so the founders lose control of a business they built, and the accounts become public for competitors to read.* — the other side
steps.note: balance, developed

steps.text: *A £1,170,000 loan at 7% costs £81,900 a year in interest, payable whether or not the factory works, but the founders keep every share.* — the other side, applied
steps.note: numbers make it concrete

steps.text: *On balance the loan is better here, because £1.17m is within ordinary borrowing range while floating would hand over part of the whole business to raise it.* — a judgement
steps.note: comes down on one side

steps.text: *It depends on how confident the owners are in demand: if sales are uncertain, the flotation's lack of repayments matters more than the loss of control.* — level 3
steps.note: says what it depends on, and how it would change

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Internal (organic)** growth: the business grows itself, through **new products** (innovation, research and development) or **new markets** (the marketing mix, technology, expanding overseas).
- **External (inorganic)** growth: a **merger**, agreed by both, or a **takeover**, buying a controlling interest, which may be hostile.
- A growing business may become a **public limited company**, whose shares anyone can buy.
- **Internal finance**: retained profit and selling assets. **External finance**: loan capital and share capital, including **stock market flotation**.
- Aims change **in response to** market conditions, technology, performance, legislation and internal reasons.
- Aims change **by** switching between survival and growth, entering or exiting markets, growing or reducing the workforce, and increasing or decreasing the product range.
- **Globalisation** brings imports, exports, changing locations and multinationals. Businesses compete internationally through **e-commerce** and by **changing the marketing mix**.
- **Barriers**: a **tariff** is a tax on imports; a **trade bloc** is a group of countries trading freely with each other.
- **Ethics** trade off against profit; the **environment and sustainability** trade off against profit. **Pressure groups** can force changes to any part of the marketing mix.
- Case figures: retained profit £350,000, internal sources £830,000, flotation £3,500,000, tariff £108 on a £900 bike.

questions.prompt: Explain one way in which globalisation could benefit a small British clothing manufacturer, and one way it could threaten it.
questions.solution: One benefit is exports. Globalisation gives the manufacturer access to overseas markets, and selling through its own website means it can reach customers in other countries without opening premises there, which increases the number of people who might buy and so raises revenue. One threat is imports. The same openness lets overseas manufacturers with lower labour costs sell into Britain at prices the small firm cannot match, which takes away its customers and forces it either to cut its price and lose margin or to compete on something other than price, such as design or British manufacture.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): some knowledge with little business terminology, limited application to the business, few connections between points, and a conclusion resting on generic assertions

Level 2 (3 to 4): mostly accurate knowledge with terminology in places, sound application to the business though not always consistent, chains of reasoning that connect points, and a conclusion based on sound evaluation

Level 3 (5 to 6): accurate knowledge and terminology throughout, detailed application to the business throughout, detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning, and a valid, well-reasoned conclusion

criteria.text: Reaches level 1: some accurate knowledge, applied at least a little, with a conclusion of some kind
Reaches level 2: sound application to this business, with chains of reasoning and a supported conclusion
Reaches level 3: accurate and detailed throughout, with logical chains and a well-reasoned conclusion

questions.modelAnswer:
**A benefit: exports.** Globalisation opens overseas markets to the manufacturer. Selling through its own website means it can reach customers in France or Germany **without opening premises there**, so the number of people who might buy rises sharply and revenue with it.

**A threat: imports.** The same openness works both ways. Manufacturers overseas with **much lower labour costs** can sell into Britain at prices a small British firm cannot match. That takes customers away and leaves the firm with a choice: cut its price and lose margin, or compete on something other than price, such as design, quality or the fact that it is made in Britain.

questions.prompt: A growing manufacturer needs £2,000,000 for a second factory. Its internal sources raise £830,000. Justify whether it should raise the shortfall through a loan or through a stock market flotation.
questions.solution: The shortfall is one million one hundred and seventy thousand pounds, since two million less the eight hundred and thirty thousand raised internally leaves that to find. A loan of that size is within reach of a bank, and its great advantage is that the founders keep every share, so they keep full control of a business they built and keep all of the future profit. The cost is interest, payable every month whether or not the second factory fills, which is a real risk because a new factory takes time to reach capacity, and missed repayments can end a business that is otherwise profitable. A flotation raises far more, needs no repayments and carries no interest, so the business is not squeezed if demand is slow to arrive, and it would raise more than the shortfall, leaving money for the machinery as well. Against that, anyone can buy the shares, so the founders lose control, the accounts become public for competitors to read, and shareholders press for profit now rather than investment for later. On balance the loan is the better choice here, because the shortfall is only a little over a million rather than the full two million and is therefore within ordinary borrowing range, so giving away ownership of the whole business to raise it would be a very high price. It depends on how confident the owners are about demand: if orders are uncertain, the flotation's lack of repayments would matter more than the loss of control.

questions.prompt: Evaluate whether a successful UK bike manufacturer should grow by taking over a rival or by expanding overseas on its own.
questions.solution: A takeover is external growth and its great attraction is speed. Buying a rival brings its customers, its staff, its premises and its share of the market in a single move, rather than building all of that over several years, and it removes a competitor at the same time, which strengthens the manufacturer's position in the UK market straight away. The costs are large and the risks real. A takeover has to be paid for, usually by borrowing or by issuing shares, so it either loads the business with interest or dilutes its ownership, and the usual reason takeovers disappoint is that two workforces used to different ways of working do not fit together, so the savings expected never appear. Expanding overseas on its own is organic growth, which is slower but stays under control. The manufacturer keeps its own culture and all of the profit, and it can start small, selling through e-commerce into one country and expanding only if it works, which limits what it can lose. The drawbacks are that growth is slow, so a competitor growing by takeover may get there first, and that selling abroad brings tariffs, which make its bikes dearer than locally made ones, and the cost of changing the marketing mix for each country. On balance the manufacturer should expand overseas organically, because it is already successful and therefore has retained profit to fund it, and because the risk is contained: a country that does not work can be abandoned, whereas a takeover that fails cannot be undone. It depends on how quickly the market is consolidating. If rivals are being bought up and the chance to acquire will not come again, the speed of a takeover may be worth its risk.

questions.prompt: Explain one reason a business might change its aim from growth to survival, and one way that change would show in its objectives.
questions.solution: One reason is a change in market conditions. A recession cuts customers' incomes, so demand for what the business sells falls, revenue falls with it and the business may struggle to cover its fixed costs, which makes staying in business a more pressing aim than getting bigger. One way that change would show is in the workforce. Having aimed to hire, the business would instead reduce the workforce, cutting the wage bill so that its costs fall in line with the lower revenue and it can keep paying what it owes. It might equally show in the product range, cutting back to the lines that still sell, or in exiting a market it can no longer afford to serve.

examTechnique.body:
Topic 2.1 is where Theme 2 starts, and the Paper 2 case study almost always has a growth decision in it. Three habits carry the marks.

**Use both names.** Edexcel writes *internal (organic)* and *external (inorganic)*. Use the pair and you cannot be marked down for the wrong one.

**Do the calculation even when the question says explain.** Retained profit, the shortfall, what a flotation raises, a tariff: these are single lines of arithmetic that turn a general answer into an applied one. Quote the figures from the case.

**Chains, then a judgement with a condition.** A 9 or 12 marker wants *because … which means … so …* ending at the business, on both sides, and then a judgement that says **what it depends on** and how the answer would change. A judgement with no condition attached caps the answer a level below.

Watch the wording of the question stem. *State* wants one thing and no explanation. *Explain* wants a chain. *Justify* and *evaluate* want both sides and a decision.
examinerErrors: Confusing a merger with a takeover. A merger is agreed by both sides; a takeover is one business buying a controlling interest, which may be hostile.
Calling retained profit just profit. It is what is left after tax and after dividends have been paid.
Listing loan capital or share capital as internal sources. The internal sources are retained profit and selling assets.
Describing a tariff as a tax on exports. It is a tax on imports, charged by the country the goods arrive in.
Saying a trade bloc bans trade. It is a group of countries trading freely with each other, with a common tariff on goods from outside.
Writing about globalisation in general instead of about the business in the case.
Giving a judgement with no condition attached. The top level needs what it depends on and how the answer would change.
Treating growth as automatically good. Fast growth can outrun a business's cash and its management.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer uses Edexcel's own pairs, internal (organic) and external (inorganic), and knows that a merger is agreed while a takeover buys a controlling interest. It does the arithmetic without being asked: retained profit, the shortfall, what a flotation raises, the tariff on a unit. On a 9 or 12 marker it builds developed chains on both sides, every one applied to the business in the case rather than to businesses in general, and then comes down on one side with a judgement that names the condition it rests on and says how the answer would change if that condition were different. On ethics it treats the issue as a trade-off with a cost, not as a slogan, and can say which part of the marketing mix a pressure group would hit.
